extracted.intended_audience: administrative law scholars, appellate practitioners, and judges considering §2401(a) accrual and APA notice-and-comment challenges
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis of when 28 U.S.C. § 2401(a)'s six-year limitations period accrues for APA challenges (notice-and-comment, arbitrary-and-capricious), and how doctrines like citizen petitions, reopening, constructive reopening, and equitable tolling affect timeliness — applied to Alliance for Hippocratic Medicine v. FDA (AHM).

rubrics_metrics.name: Accrual of 28 U.S.C. § 2401(a) for APA claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The six-year clock of 28 U.S.C. § 2401(a) starts when 'the right of action first accrues.' For APA claims, courts of appeals agree accrual occurs when a rule is promulgated — the moment the administrative procedure illegality is complete (the agency action is 'without observance of procedure required by law').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supported by statutory text and APA provisions (5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(D)); courts (Corner Post, Rettig, Sierra Club v. Slater, etc.) hold accrual at promulgation. Example: challenges to a 2000 approval accrue at that approval; Abbott Labs v. Gardner is instructive. The transgression (inadequate notice-and-comment, failure to consider evidence, failure to respond to comments) is complete at promulgation, and the claim is available to all eligible plaintiffs at that time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public-nature rule: accrual is the same for all plaintiffs
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrative procedure gives a public right to participate in agency decisionmaking; because the injury from failure to follow procedure is 'incurred by all persons' at the time of promulgation, the right of action accrues for all plaintiffs when any plaintiff can sue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Herr v. U.S. Forest Service, Shiny Rock Mining Corp., and administrative law treatises. This undergirds the earlier-accrual rule and distinguishes APA public-right claims from individualized application claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory/constitutional limit: APA claims barred when limitations preclude judicial review
rubrics_metrics.description: The APA (5 U.S.C. § 701(a)(1)) provides that claims cannot be made when a limitations period 'precludes judicial review'; absent a more specific limitations period, § 2401(a) supplies a six-year default.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy implications include stability and reliance; limitations periods are classic tools to protect finality and reliance interests, and thus the default six-year bar is meaningful for administrative procedure challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wind River exception: later accrual for claims challenging substantive statutory authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The accrual rule differs for claims that a regulation exceeds the authority of its substantive authorizing statute; in such cases later accrual may apply (e.g., Wind River Mining Corp. v. U.S.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish public-right procedural claims (accrue at promulgation) from statutory-authority challenges (accrual may occur when the claimant is injured by the regulation's application).

rubrics_metrics.name: Citizen petitions generally do not extend the limitations period
rubrics_metrics.description: Filing a citizen/administrative petition does not automatically restart or extend the six-year limitations period for challenging the original rule; administrative petitions typically produce a separate final agency action (petition denial) which is subject to its own judicial review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: McAfee v. U.S. FDA and appellate precedents show petition denials are distinct final actions. Allowing petitions to reopen stale challenges would permit plaintiffs to leverage petitions into an 'infinite ability' to challenge old administrative procedure errors. The review should focus on the petition record, not the original rulemaking record, and the typical remedy is remand rather than invalidation of the original rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and standard of review for citizen petition denials
rubrics_metrics.description: Judicial review of a citizen petition denial is governed by the arbitrary-and-capricious standard and is typically extremely deferential; review should be confined to the petition record rather than the administrative record for the original rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases like McAfee and Graceway Pharm. confine review to the petition record and apply a deferential arbitrary-and-capricious review; Tummino and other decisions illustrate that courts usually remand petition denials to the agency rather than invalidate the original rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive reopening doctrine and its prerequisites
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Constructive reopening' applies only when an agency change 'significantly alters the stakes of judicial review' and is one that 'could not have been reasonably anticipated' — a magnitude often described as a 'sea change.' It is a D.C. Circuit doctrine the Supreme Court has not fully embraced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Developed in Kennecott and applied in Sierra Club v. EPA and related D.C. Circuit cases; a showing of a 'sea change' or unexpected, significant alteration is required. AHM's facts (March 2016 Amendments) do not meet this standard because the amendments did not change basic prerequisites and were reasonably anticipated.

rubrics_metrics.name: How agencies reopen an issue (straightforward reopening)
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency reopens an issue by holding out the unchanged section as a proposed regulation, offering an explanation for its language, soliciting comments on its substance, and responding to the comments in promulgating the regulation in final form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited framework from Am. Iron & Steel Inst. v. EPA; straightforward reopening is distinguishable from constructive reopening and requires clear agency-initiated reconsideration in the rulemaking process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equitable tolling is available but limited; petition consideration alone usually won't toll
rubrics_metrics.description: Equitable tolling can extend statute of limitations in extraordinary circumstances (e.g., agency error or misleading conduct), but extended consideration of a citizen petition ordinarily does not constitute the kind of error that supports equitable tolling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare Irwin (equitable tolling denied where no relevant notice) and Socop-Gonzalez (equitable tolling granted where official gave incorrect advice). In AHM, time spent by FDA considering the petition does not prevent filing and, given statutory provisions that deem petitions denied after a period, does not justify tolling to reach otherwise untimely challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: FDA-specific 150-day deemed denial rule for citizen petitions (21 U.S.C. § 505(q)(2)(A))
rubrics_metrics.description: Under 21 U.S.C. § 505(q)(2)(A), an FDA citizen petition is deemed denied 150 days after filing if not acted on, which can create a discrete, relatively short extension before a plaintiff's ability to sue is unblocked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if deemed denial extends the window, it only shifts the deadline modestly (e.g., from March 2022 to June 2022 in AHM), and may still leave a later-filed suit untimely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affirmative defense of statute of limitations can be preserved despite pleading defects
rubrics_metrics.description: A limitations period defense may be preserved even when technical errors are made in pleading, so long as the plaintiff had notice of the defense and was not unfairly surprised or prejudiced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Fed. R. Civ. P. 8(c), Smith v. Travelers, Tahoe-Sierra; courts may treat vague or late-invoked limitations defenses as preserved if the plaintiff had sufficient notice and no unfair surprise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance interests and policy of stability support earlier accrual
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations periods promote stability and protect diverse reliance interests (patients, providers, pharmaceutical industry, investors); these reliance considerations support applying an earlier-accrual rule for procedural challenges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy discussion: statutes of limitations serve 'peace' and finality; invalidating long-settled agency actions would disrupt regulatory frameworks and business and investment decisions (briefs of pharma industry and amici illustrate these stakes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical remedy for petition-related review is remand, not invalidation of the original rule
rubrics_metrics.description: When courts review a citizen petition denial, the usual remedial response is to remand the petition to the agency for reconsideration rather than to invalidate the underlying original regulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tummino and Graceway Pharm. demonstrate remand as the typical remedy after finding error in petition disposition; this limits the scope of relief available to petitioners seeking to use petitions to unwind older rulemakings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application to Alliance for Hippocratic Medicine (AHM) timeline
rubrics_metrics.description: In AHM, the relevant six-year window runs back from the complaint filing date (November 18, 2022), so only FDA actions after November 18, 2016 are challengable; the 2000 Approval and March 2016 Petition Denial/Amendments are therefore time-barred, while the 2021 Petition Denial and 2021 Non-Enforcement Decision are timely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factual application: Fifth Circuit correctly time-barred challenges to the 2000 Approval and 2016 Petition Denial; the court incorrectly assumed away the time-bar as to the March 2016 Amendments by relying on party agreement rather than a substantive waiver record. The Supreme Court should analyze whether the March 2016 Amendments are untimely and treat intervening petition denials as separate actions subject to deferential review.
